e.etymology: A 20th-century spelling of Stacy, which for girls began as a short form of Anastasia, from Greek anastasis, resurrection. For boys Stacy came from Eustace.
A spelling of Mamie, the old pet form of Mary and Margaret, sometimes also linked to May.
A pet form of Sandra, Alexandra and Cassandra. Sandra itself is short for Alexandra, from Greek words meaning to defend and man.
A spelling of Dwayne or Duane, from the Irish surname Ó Dubháin, descendant of Dubhán, a pet form of dubh, dark or black.
A spelling of Melvin, a variant of the Scottish surname Melville, which comes from Malleville, a place in Normandy.
A Spanish spelling of Hortensia, the feminine of the Roman family name Hortensius, from Latin hortus, garden. Hortensia is also the Spanish word for the hydrangea.
A surname of unexplained origin taken up as a first name, mostly in the American South in the early 20th century.
A shortened spelling of William, common in old records. William comes from Old High German Willahelm, joining the words for will and helmet.
A pet-form spelling alongside Lanny; the fuller name behind it varies from family to family.
A pet form of Eugenie and Eugenia, and of Eugene and Gene for men, all from Greek eugenes, well-born.

assoc.t: a genie, the wish-granting spirit of the lamp

e.note: Spelled the same as genie, the wish-granting spirit, so expect lamp and Aladdin jokes.

e.etymology: Beth and Ann written as one name. Beth is short for Elizabeth, and Ann is the English form of Hebrew Hannah.
From the surname Prentiss or Prentice, from Middle English prentis, apprentice.
The short form of Lewis, the English form of Louis, from the Germanic name Chlodovech, famous in battle. In Polish, Lew is a separate name meaning lion.
namesakes: Lew Alcindor (birth name of Kareem Abdul-Jabbar)
Lew Wallace (Civil War general and author of Ben-Hur)

e.etymology: In mid-century American use, a spelling of Brenda. Brinda is also an Indian name, a form of Sanskrit Vrinda, a name of the sacred tulsi or holy basil plant.
The short form of Victor, Latin for conqueror, and occasionally of Victoria.
namesakes: Vic Morrow (actor in the TV series Combat!)

e.etymology: An American name of the early 1900s whose source is unclear. Today Euna is also a romanized form of the Korean name Eun-a.
Came into use in the late 2000s after House of Deréon, the fashion line of Beyoncé and her mother, named for Beyoncé's grandmother Agnèz Deréon, a Louisiana Creole.
A pet form of Agnes, from Greek hagnos, pure or chaste, and of Agatha, from Greek agathos, good.

assoc.t: Aggies, the students and teams of Texas A&M University

e.etymology: From an English and Irish surname that began as a patronymic of Hardy or of Germanic names built on hard, brave or tough. Use as a first name peaked with Warren G. Harding's 1920 election.
A variant of Antoinette, the French feminine pet form of Antoine, or Anthony, which goes back to the Roman family name Antonius.
A spelling of Bonnie, from the Scots word bonny, pretty or fine, which goes back to French bon, good.
A short form of Margaret, from Greek margarites, pearl, and of Megan, the Welsh pet form of Margaret.
namesakes: Meg Ryan (actress in When Harry Met Sally and Sleepless in Seattle)
Meg March (eldest sister in Little Women)

assoc.t: Meg, the put-upon daughter on Family Guy
Meg March, the eldest sister in Little Women
Meg (Megara), the heroine of Disney's Hercules

e.etymology: A spelling of Chelsea, the London district whose Old English name joins cealc, chalk, and hyth, landing place.
A spelling of Kristin, borrowed in the 20th century from the Norwegian form of Christina, from Latin Christianus, a follower of Christ.
namesakes: Krysten Ritter (star of Jessica Jones and Breaking Bad)

e.etymology: From the name of the Shawnee people, which comes from their own word saawanwa and is linked to a word for southerners.
namesakes: Shawnee Smith (actress in the Saw films and Becker)

assoc.t: the Shawnee, a Native American nation

e.note: It is the name of a living Native American nation, which some families will want to weigh before using it.

e.etymology: A spelling of Destiny, the English word for fate, from Old French destinée and Latin destinare, to determine.
A spelling of Marilyn, a 20th-century blend of Mary and Lynn.
A form of Reynard, from the Germanic name Raginhard, counsel plus hardy. Reynard the Fox was so well known in medieval tales that renard became the French word for fox.
A spelling of Edith, from Old English Eadgyth, joining ead, wealth or fortune, and gyth, war.
A form of Celeste, from Latin caelestis, heavenly. The celesta is also a keyboard instrument with a bell-like tone.
An American name of the La- family that rose in 1977, the year LeVar Burton starred in the miniseries Roots.
namesakes: LeVar Burton (Reading Rainbow host and Star Trek actor)
LaVar Ball (outspoken father of NBA players Lonzo and LaMelo Ball)
e.note: Lavar is the Spanish verb meaning to wash.

assoc.t: LaVar Ball, outspoken father of NBA players

e.etymology: A spelling of Mary found in old records. Mary comes through Latin and Greek Maria from Hebrew Miryam, whose meaning is uncertain.
e.note: It is spelled like the verb marry, so it will usually be read as a word or corrected to Mary.
